name: Brain Waves & Sleep Stages
cards: Alpha wave frequency?
8 to 13 cycles per second.
When do healthy adults show alpha waves?
Awake in a quiet, resting state.
Where are alpha waves most intense?
In the occipital region.
What happens to alpha waves in deep sleep?
Alpha waves disappear.
Beta wave frequency?
Greater than 14 cycles per second, as high as 80.
Where are beta waves mainly recorded?
Parietal and frontal regions during their activation.
Beta wave voltage and synchrony?
Low voltage and asynchronous.
Mental state that beta waves reflect?
Awake, alert, and actively processing information.
Awake person turns attention to a mental task: what happens to alpha waves?
They stop and are replaced by beta waves.
Awake with eyes closed and relaxed: which wave?
Alpha waves (quiet wakefulness).
Awake with eyes open, alert and active: which wave?
Beta waves (alert wakefulness).
Theta wave frequency?
4 to 7 cycles per second.
Where do theta waves occur in children?
Parietal and temporal regions.
Emotional state that brings theta waves in some adults?
Stress, especially disappointment and frustration.
Brain disorders that show theta waves?
Many, especially degenerative brain states.
Delta wave frequency?
Less than 3.5 cycles per second.
Delta wave voltage compared with other brain waves?
Often 2 to 4 times greater.
Where do delta waves arise?
In the cortex, independent of lower brain regions.
When do delta waves occur?
Very deep sleep, infancy, and serious organic brain disease.
Which non-rapid eye movement stages show theta waves?
Stages N1 and N2.
Which wave marks stage N3?
Delta waves (deep sleep).
Which wave marks rapid eye movement sleep?
Beta waves, like the awake state.
Rapid eye movement sleep electroencephalogram pattern?
Mixed, low-voltage pattern with sawtooth waves.
Rapid eye movement sleep waves: rhythm and frequency?
Irregular and high frequency.
Why is rapid eye movement sleep called desynchronized sleep?
Neuron firing lacks synchrony during brain activity.
Why is rapid eye movement sleep called paradoxical sleep?
Its brain wave pattern resembles wakefulness.
Eye movements in rapid eye movement sleep?
Irregular, sharply peaked eye movements.
Electroencephalogram frequency as sleep deepens?
It becomes progressively slower.
Electroencephalogram voltage in light sleep (stage N1)?
Voltage becomes low.
Stage N1 description?
Transition from wakefulness; drowsy, light sleep.
Longest sleep stage by total duration?
Stage N2, the majority of the cycle.
Stage N2: heart rate and temperature?
They both decrease.
Deepest non-rapid eye movement stage?
Stage N3 (deep sleep).
Stage when body tissue growth and repair occurs?
Stage N3 (deep sleep).
How does stage N3 change with age?
It decreases with age.

name: Sleep States, Cycles & Functions
cards: Unconsciousness that sensory or other stimuli can reverse: sleep or coma?
Sleep: the person can be aroused.
Unconsciousness that no stimulus can reverse: sleep or coma?
Coma: the person cannot be aroused.
Average nightly sleep?
About 8 hours.
Sleep cycles per night?
4 to 5 cycles.
Length of one sleep cycle?
90 to 120 minutes.
Deep, restful type of sleep?
Non-rapid eye movement sleep.
Restfulness of rapid eye movement sleep?
Not restful or deep.
Share of a young adult's sleep spent in rapid eye movement sleep?
About 25% of sleep time.
How often does a rapid eye movement episode recur?
About every 90 minutes.
Length of one rapid eye movement episode?
5 to 30 minutes.
Rapid eye movement episodes when extremely sleepy?
Short or even absent.
Rapid eye movement episodes as a person becomes more rested?
They grow longer.
Sleep type linked to vivid dreaming?
Rapid eye movement sleep.
Brain metabolism in rapid eye movement sleep?
Up by as much as 20%.
Muscle tone in rapid eye movement sleep?
Atonia of voluntary muscles except eyes and diaphragm.
What does the muscle atonia of rapid eye movement sleep reflect?
Inhibition of spinal muscle control areas.
Heart and breathing rates in rapid eye movement sleep?
Irregular, typical of the dream state.
Can people wake spontaneously from rapid eye movement sleep?
Yes, in the morning.
Blood pressure, heart rate, breathing and metabolism in non-rapid eye movement sleep?
Fall by 10% to 30%.
Autonomic tone in non-rapid eye movement sleep?
Increased parasympathetic tone.
Peripheral vascular tone in non-rapid eye movement sleep?
It is decreased.
Do dreams occur in non-rapid eye movement sleep?
Yes, dreams and nightmares can occur.
How do rapid eye movement dreams differ from non-rapid eye movement dreams?
More bodily muscle activity.
Why are non-rapid eye movement dreams often forgotten?
They are not consolidated in memory.
Dream vividness in non-rapid eye movement sleep?
Less vivid dreams.
Two major types of physiological effects of sleep?
On the nervous system and on other body systems.
Sleep function that clears the brain?
Clearance of metabolic waste from neural activity.
Sleep function that prunes synapses?
Targeted erasure of synapses holding unimportant information.
Sleep function for energy?
Conservation of metabolic energy.
Developmental and cognitive functions of sleep?
Neural maturation, learning and memory, cognition.
Effect of a few days of sleep restriction?
Lower cognitive and physical performance, productivity, and health.
Are the specific functions of sleep fully understood?
No, they remain a mystery.
Nuclei that drive wakefulness when sleep centers are inactive?
Mesencephalic and upper pontile reticular activating nuclei.
What sustains wakefulness once it begins?
Positive feedback between reticular activating nuclei and cortex.
Why does wakefulness give way to sleep?
Activating neurons fatigue and the feedback cycle fades.
